write.desc: This topic defines the Riemann integral of a bounded function on [a,b] through the supremum and infimum of Darboux sums, proves which functions are integrable and which are not, develops the properties of the integral, and links integration to differentiation through the fundamental theorem of calculus and its consequences (substitution, parts, the integral Taylor remainder, improper integrals and the integral test).

points.name: Partitions and upper and lower Darboux sums
points.what: The learner can define a partition of [a,b] and the upper and lower sums U(f,P) and L(f,P) of a bounded function using the supremum and infimum of f on each subinterval, and compute them for simple functions such as step functions and x^2.
outside: supremum and infimum of a bounded set of real numbers
bounded functions

points.name: Refinements and why every lower sum is below every upper sum
points.what: The learner can prove that refining a partition raises lower sums and lowers upper sums, and deduce that L(f,P) <= U(f,Q) for any two partitions P and Q by passing to a common refinement.
outside: the supremum of a subset is at most the supremum of the whole set

points.name: Upper and lower integrals and the definition of Riemann integrability
points.what: The learner can define the upper integral as the infimum of all upper sums and the lower integral as the supremum of all lower sums, show the lower integral never exceeds the upper one, and define f to be Riemann integrable when they are equal, the common value being the integral.
outside: completeness axiom: every nonempty bounded set has a supremum and infimum

points.name: The Riemann (epsilon) criterion for integrability
points.what: The learner can prove that a bounded f is integrable exactly when for every epsilon > 0 there is a partition P with U(f,P) - L(f,P) < epsilon, and uses this criterion as the standard tool for proving integrability.
outside: epsilon characterisation of supremum and infimum
the 'a <= b + epsilon for every epsilon > 0 implies a <= b' argument

points.name: A non-integrable function: the Dirichlet function
points.what: The learner can show that the indicator function of the rationals on [a,b] has every lower sum 0 and every upper sum b - a, so it is bounded but not Riemann integrable.
outside: density of the rationals and irrationals in the reals

points.name: Continuous functions on [a,b] are integrable
points.what: The learner can prove, using uniform continuity and the Riemann criterion, that every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is integrable, choosing a partition fine enough that the oscillation on each piece is less than epsilon/(b-a).
outside: uniform continuity of continuous functions on closed bounded intervals (Heine-Cantor theorem)

points.name: Monotone functions on [a,b] are integrable
points.what: The learner can prove that every monotone function on [a,b] is integrable with a uniform partition, where U - L telescopes to (f(b) - f(a))(b - a)/n, even though such a function may have infinitely many discontinuities.

points.name: Bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities
points.what: The learner can prove that a bounded function continuous except at finitely many points is integrable, by enclosing each discontinuity in a short subinterval, and deduce that changing a function at finitely many points does not change its integral.

points.name: Thomae's function is integrable
points.what: The learner can prove that Thomae's function (1/q at p/q in lowest terms, 0 at irrationals) is integrable on [0,1] with integral 0, using that only finitely many points have value at least epsilon, an example of an integrable function discontinuous at every rational.

points.name: Linearity of the integral
points.what: The learner can prove that if f and g are integrable then f + g and cf are integrable with the integral of f + g equal to the sum of the integrals and the integral of cf equal to c times the integral, handling sup(f+g) <= sup f + sup g and the sign of c.

points.name: Additivity over intervals
points.what: The learner can prove that f is integrable on [a,b] if and only if it is integrable on [a,c] and [c,b], with the integral over [a,b] the sum of the two, and uses the conventions for an integral from b to a and from a to a.

points.name: Products and compositions with continuous functions
points.what: The learner can prove that if f is integrable with values in [m,M] and phi is continuous on [m,M] then phi composed with f is integrable, and deduce that |f|, f^2 and the product fg of integrable functions are integrable.
outside: uniform continuity of continuous functions on closed bounded intervals (Heine-Cantor theorem)

points.name: Monotonicity of the integral and the triangle inequality for integrals
points.what: The learner can prove that f <= g implies the integral of f is at most that of g, that m(b-a) <= integral of f <= M(b-a) when m <= f <= M, and that the absolute value of the integral of f is at most the integral of |f|.

points.name: The mean value theorem for integrals
points.what: The learner can prove that a continuous f on [a,b] takes its average value (1/(b-a)) times its integral at some point c, and the weighted version with a nonnegative integrable weight g, and knows why continuity is needed.
outside: extreme value theorem
intermediate value theorem

points.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus: evaluating an integral by an antiderivative
points.what: The learner can prove that if F is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and F' = f is integrable, then the integral of f over [a,b] equals F(b) - F(a), by applying the mean value theorem on each subinterval of a partition, and knows that integrability of F' must be assumed.
outside: mean value theorem for derivatives

points.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus: differentiating an integral in its upper limit
points.what: The learner can prove that for integrable f the function G(x) = integral of f from a to x is Lipschitz and hence continuous, and that G'(c) = f(c) at every point c where f is continuous, so every continuous function has an antiderivative.
outside: derivative defined as a limit of difference quotients
epsilon-delta definition of continuity at a point

points.name: Integration by parts as a theorem
points.what: The learner can state integration by parts with its hypotheses (f and g differentiable with integrable derivatives) and prove it from the product rule and the evaluation form of the fundamental theorem.
outside: product rule for derivatives

points.name: Integration by substitution as a theorem
points.what: The learner can state the change of variables formula with its hypotheses (g continuously differentiable on [a,b], f continuous on the image of g) and prove it by differentiating the composition of an antiderivative of f with g.
outside: chain rule

points.name: Taylor's theorem with the integral form of the remainder
points.what: The learner can prove by repeated integration by parts that if f has n+1 continuous derivatives the error f(x) - P_n(x) equals the integral from a to x of f^(n+1)(t)(x-t)^n/n!, and use it to bound the error of a Taylor polynomial.
outside: Taylor polynomial of a function at a point
higher derivatives
proof by induction

points.name: Improper integrals and the comparison test
points.what: The learner can define integrals over unbounded intervals and of functions unbounded near an endpoint as limits of integrals, decide that the integral of 1/x^p converges on [1, infinity) exactly when p > 1 and on (0,1] exactly when p < 1, and prove the comparison test for nonnegative integrands.
outside: limits of functions at infinity and one-sided limits
a monotone bounded function has a limit at infinity

points.name: The integral test for series
points.what: The learner can prove that for a positive decreasing f on [1, infinity) the series of f(n) converges exactly when the improper integral of f converges, by comparing partial sums with upper and lower sums, and apply it to settle the p-series and series such as the sum of 1/(n log n).
outside: a series with nonnegative terms converges if and only if its partial sums are bounded
p-series

points.name: Riemann sums with tags as an equivalent definition
points.what: The learner can define tagged partitions, Riemann sums and the mesh of a partition, and understands (with the key step of the proof) that f is integrable with integral I exactly when Riemann sums approach I as the mesh goes to 0, the definition used in many other textbooks.

points.name: Lebesgue's criterion for Riemann integrability (stated)
points.what: The learner can define a set of measure zero, show that countable sets have measure zero, and state without proof that a bounded function on [a,b] is Riemann integrable exactly when its set of discontinuities has measure zero, checking it against the Dirichlet, Thomae and monotone examples.
outside: countable sets
discontinuities of monotone functions are countable

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 7: The Riemann Integral (7.2 definition and criterion, 7.3 integrating discontinuous functions, 7.4 properties, 7.5 fundamental theorem, 7.6 Lebesgue's criterion)

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Chapter 7: The Riemann Integral (tagged-sum definition, integrable functions, fundamental theorem, the Darboux integral); Chapter 10 for improper (generalized) integrals

where.title: Michael Spivak, Calculus
where.detail: Chapter 13: Integrals; Chapter 14: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; Chapter 19 for substitution and parts; Chapter 23 for the integral test

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 6: The Riemann-Stieltjes Integral (take the integrator alpha(x) = x)

where.title: Kenneth A. Ross, Elementary Analysis: The Theory of Calculus
where.detail: Sections 32-34 (Darboux integral, properties, fundamental theorem) and Section 36 (improper integrals)
